sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Reference ranges are built backwards from healthy people, not from sick ones. Researchers measure a large group known to be well, see where the middle 95 percent of their values land, and call that span 'normal.' So the range is a description of health, not a rule about disease, which is why it shifts when the group being described changes.

### Question 2

A single measurement is a dot; a baseline turns later measurements into a line. Knowing a patient's usual blood pressure is 148 systolic changes what today's 118 means, even though 118 by itself looks unremarkable. The first set of numbers is not interesting for what it says, but for what it lets every later number say.

### Question 3

The dividing line is verifiability, not truthfulness. Only the patient can feel the nausea, so it stays subjective no matter how accurate it is; anyone in the room can read the same thermometer, so that stays objective even if the device is miscalibrated. Both categories are real cues, and the strongest assessments pair them.

### Question 4

Cardiac output is a product of two numbers, so if one goes up the other can come down without changing the result. A conditioned heart moves more blood per beat, so it needs fewer beats per minute to deliver the same total. The rate looks low against the population range, but the quantity that actually matters, blood delivered per minute, is normal.

### Question 5

Expected aging is population-wide and slow; abnormality is individual and out of proportion. Nearly every 80-year-old has stiffer arteries and a slower maximal heart rate, so those findings need no explanation beyond age. A finding that most healthy 80-year-olds do not share still needs a cause, and calling it 'just aging' is how treatable problems get missed.

### Question 6

Every measurement contains noise plus signal. Noise scatters in both directions and cancels out over time, so one odd value is usually noise. Movement that keeps going the same direction across several measurements cannot be explained by scatter, which is why direction over time is more informative than any one reading's distance from normal.

### Question 7

Comparing a number to a range only works if the number was produced under the same conditions the range describes. A rate counted after walking is answering a different question than the resting range was built to answer. Rechecking after rest does not discard the finding; it converts it into something comparable, and how fast it settles is itself useful information.

### Question 8

Aging changes cognition on a scale of years; this change happened over hours. Timescale alone rules out aging as the explanation, which is why acute mental status change is treated as a physiologic alarm rather than a baseline shift. In older adults it is often the earliest and sometimes the only sign of infection or low oxygen.

### Question 9

Autoregulation adapts to whatever pressure an organ has been receiving for years. Kidneys and brain accustomed to a systolic of 150 are tuned to that supply, so dropping to 118 removes a margin they were relying on. The number is normal for the population and low for this person, and organs respond to the second comparison.

### Question 10

Two findings that share a mechanism carry more weight together than the sum of their individual weights. Low urine output alone has many causes, and a slightly faster pulse alone has many causes, but reduced perfusion explains both at once and explains why they are moving together. Cue clustering is the habit of asking what single problem would produce this whole set.

### Question 11

A normal blood pressure during shock is not evidence that nothing is wrong; it can be evidence that the body is working hard to keep it there. Compensation is an active process with a finite budget, and the measured value stays flat while the budget is being spent. The number changes only when the budget runs out, so it is a late indicator, not an early one.

### Question 12

The flag is generated by arithmetic, not by clinical judgment; the computer only knows whether the number crossed a statistical boundary. Since that boundary was drawn to exclude 5 percent of healthy people, some flags are simply the price of testing. The flag earns your attention, and the patient's history and symptoms decide what it means.
